title: Transient Occupancy Tax
summary: Measure F asks City of Mountain View voters to authorize the City Council to raise the city's Transient Occupancy Tax (hotel/short-term-rental tax) from its current 10%, unchanged since 1991, to a voter-approved ceiling of 15%. The measure itself does not set any new rate; it only grants the Council authority to adopt an ordinance raising the rate, in one or more steps, up to that 15% cap, whenever it chooses after the election. Revenue goes to the city's General Fund and is projected at up to about $5.2 million a year if the Council eventually reaches the full 15%.
what_it_really_means: Unlike Gilroy's Measure B on the same county ballot, which immediately raises that city's hotel tax to a specific rate (11%) and lets the Council adjust it from there, Mountain View's Measure F changes nothing about the tax rate itself. Per the City Attorney's Impartial Analysis: "A 'yes' vote would amend the Mountain View City Code to authorize the City Council to increase the Transient Occupancy Tax rate up to a maximum of 15%. A 'no' vote would reject the proposed ordinance, and the Transient Occupancy Tax rate would remain at 10%." The ordinance text attached to the City Council's resolution (amending Mountain View City Code Section 33.2) keeps the tax rate at 10% in subsection (b) and adds a new subsection (c): "Pursuant to authority granted by the voters, the City Council may, by ordinance amending this section, increase or decrease the tax rate established in subsection (b), provided that the tax rate shall not exceed fifteen percent (15%)." If Measure F passes, the rate stays at 10% the day after the election and every day after that until the Council separately adopts a new ordinance setting a different number; nothing in the measure requires the Council to ever do so, or sets a timetable for when.

City staff have already signaled the sequence: the June 23, 2026 council report that recommended placing Measure F on the ballot states under "Next Steps" that, if voters approve it, "staff will return to the Council to consider a new TOT rate" in "Nov/Dec" 2026, weeks after the election. The primary argument in favor, signed by Mayor Emily Ann Ramos and four others, confirms this is deliberate: "If voters approve Measure __, the City Council will consider implementing any new TOT rate, not to exceed the 15% cap, at a public meeting after the election." A voter cannot know from the ballot question what rate the Council will actually choose, only that it cannot exceed 15%; the $5,200,000 annual figure printed in the ballot question is the revenue estimate for that maximum, not a number this measure guarantees.

One procedural detail distinguishes Mountain View's mechanism from Gilroy's, and it is not obvious from the ballot title. Gilroy's ordinance lets its City Council change the hotel-tax rate "by resolution," a lower-friction legislative act than an ordinance. Mountain View's amended Section 33.2(c) instead requires the City Council to act "by ordinance amending this section" to raise or lower the rate. An ordinance is a more formal legislative instrument than a resolution under standard California municipal practice, but no source reviewed, including the Impartial Analysis, council report, or ordinance text itself, specifies whether Mountain View's charter requires two readings, a waiting period, or other procedural steps beyond a normal noticed council meeting for this particular ordinance amendment. The practical check on how and when the Council raises the rate is therefore political accountability at future city elections, not a supermajority vote or a mandatory additional election.

The tax applies identically to hotel and short-term-rental guests. The Impartial Analysis states plainly, "This hotel tax also applies to short-term rentals," and the ballot question itself names both: the Council is authorized to increase the tax "paid by hotel and short-term rental guests." The underlying Mountain View City Code defines "hotel" broadly and the tax is collected the same way, self-reported quarterly by the operator, for both categories; nothing in the ordinance text creates a separate rate, cap, or timeline for Airbnb-style listings versus traditional hotels and motels. Stays exceeding 30 consecutive days and occupancy by government employees on official business are exempt, per both the Impartial Analysis and the June 2026 council report.

This is a general tax whose revenue is not legally earmarked to the services the ballot question names. The Impartial Analysis states: "All revenue generated by this tax would be placed in the City's general fund and could be used for any general governmental purpose," and lists potholes, streets, police/fire/911 response, affordable housing, and parks only as "examples" of what a general governmental purpose "could" include, not as a binding list. The City Council's own resolution invokes California Government Code section 53723, the general-tax majority-vote threshold, rather than the two-thirds supermajority California requires for a special tax with a dedicated purpose; that lower bar is a direct legal consequence of the money being unrestricted General Fund revenue, the same structure Gilroy's Measure B uses.

Measure F did not begin as a hotel-tax proposal. The City's Fiscal Years 2025-26 and 2026-27 Council Work Plan called for pursuing a 2026 revenue measure, and the Council's 2026 Revenue Measure Ad Hoc Sub-Committee (drawn from the Council Finance Committee) spent from October 2025 through June 2026 developing what was originally planned as a $480-650 million general obligation bond to fund capital projects. Three rounds of polling by EMC Research and political strategist Clifford Moss, obtained by the Mountain View Voice under public records law, tracked support for that bond measure falling from 61% in January 2026 to 54% in March to 52% in May, roughly 15 points short of the two-thirds supermajority a GO bond requires; support for a smaller $495 million version fell to 42% once respondents heard opposition arguments. The consultants' own June 2026 report concluded a bond "does not appear feasible." The city pivoted to a Transient Occupancy Tax increase, which only needs a simple majority as a general tax, within about two weeks of receiving that final poll data; no hotel-tax-specific polling was conducted in 2026, and the TOT concept had last been tested by the city's pollsters in 2024, when it also considered and ultimately did not use it, opting instead for a property transfer tax increase that voters approved that November.

The City Council voted unanimously (per the Impartial Analysis, the Mountain View Voice, and the Los Altos Town Crier) to place Measure F on the ballot on June 23, 2026, and no primary argument against the measure was filed with the Registrar of Voters by the August 2026 deadline. Voters will see only the argument in favor in the County Voter Information Guide; unlike Gilroy's Measure B, where the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association filed a countywide opposition argument, no organized opposition campaign, hotel-industry opposition argument, or ballot-measure committee opposing Measure F was identified in the sources reviewed for this analysis, though at least one Mountain View Voice reader comment on the paper's July 2026 bond-polling story said they planned to vote no, arguing the tax burdens small hotel owners more than large chains.

The dollar figures in circulation come from several different baselines and are not interchangeable. The Impartial Analysis estimates each 1-percentage-point increase could generate about $1.1 million a year, which extrapolates to roughly $5.5 million at the full 5-point increase to 15%. The June 2026 council report's own forecast table puts a 5-point increase at $5.17 million to $5.39 million a year depending on fiscal year, and a San Jose Spotlight report citing city staff put the potential increase at "about $5.4 million annually." The ballot question itself, and the underlying ordinance and resolution, print "up to $5,200,000 annually." All of these describe the same hypothetical, an eventual Council decision to raise the rate the full 5 points to 15%, not a number Measure F itself locks in; if the Council raises the rate by less than the full 5 points, or not at all, actual new revenue will be lower than any of these figures, including the one printed on the ballot.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: none. This is a City of Mountain View general tax measure; it creates no state General Fund obligation.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: none mandated on the county; the City of Mountain View budgeted a $250,000 limited-period appropriation in its Fiscal Year 2025-26 budget for revenue-measure consulting services (covering both the shelved bond measure and this TOT measure), and separate election administration costs are covered in the City Clerk's Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget, per the June 23, 2026 council report.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: Increases City of Mountain View General Fund revenue, but the amount is not fixed by this measure. The city's existing 10% TOT generated roughly $11 million in Fiscal Year 2025-26, per the council report. If the City Council later raises the rate to the full 15% ceiling this measure authorizes, up to about $5.2 million a year in new revenue is projected (the figure printed in the ballot question); the City Attorney's Impartial Analysis separately estimates about $1.1 million in new revenue per 1-percentage-point increase, and the council report's own forecast table estimates $2.1 million to $5.4 million in new annual revenue for a 2-to-5-point increase. None of these figures is guaranteed by a yes vote alone, since the measure only authorizes the Council to raise the rate; it does not set a new rate or require the Council to act.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: Ongoing tax revenue for the City of Mountain View's General Fund, with no sunset date specified; the ballot question states the authorization continues "until ended by voters." The city's revenue-measure consulting and election-administration costs are one-time/annual budget items, not created by this measure specifically.
fiscal_impact.narrative: Voters approving Measure F are not voting on a dollar amount; they are voting to let the City Council decide, at an unspecified future public meeting, how much of the 10%-to-15% range to actually charge. City staff have said they plan to bring a specific new rate to the Council in November or December 2026, shortly after the election, but the measure does not require or schedule that. The up-to-$5.2-million figure printed in the ballot question, like the roughly $5.4-to-$5.5 million figures cited by city staff and the argument in favor, assumes the Council eventually adopts the full 15% rate; smaller increases would raise proportionally less, on the Impartial Analysis's estimate of about $1.1 million per percentage point. Because the tax is deposited into the General Fund as a general tax rather than a restricted account, none of these figures is legally earmarked to the specific services listed in the ballot question (potholes, police/fire/911, affordable housing, parks); the money is fungible with the rest of the city's general operating budget, per the City Attorney's Impartial Analysis.

tax_changes: Authorizes the City of Mountain View City Council to raise the city's existing Transient Occupancy Tax (hotel and short-term rental tax) from its current 10% to a ceiling of 15%, by a future ordinance the Council may adopt at its own discretion after the election; the measure itself does not change the rate, which stays at 10% unless and until the Council separately acts.

new_spending_areas: General Fund city services named in the ballot question as illustrative examples only, not a legal earmark, per the City Attorney's Impartial Analysis: repairing potholes, streets, and sidewalks; improving police, fire, and 911 emergency response services; supporting affordable housing; adding new parks; and other general government services.
spending.funding_source: Potential increase in existing Transient Occupancy Tax (hotel and short-term rental tax) revenue, paid by guests staying 30 days or less, deposited into the City of Mountain View's General Fund and usable for any lawful municipal purpose, not legally restricted to the categories named in the ballot question. No new revenue is generated unless and until the City Council separately adopts an ordinance raising the rate above the current 10%.

control_and_power: Measure F transfers no rate-setting authority immediately; it authorizes the City Council to adopt a future ordinance raising the Transient Occupancy Tax rate above its current 10%, as long as the new rate never exceeds a 15% ceiling. Unlike Gilroy's Measure B, which lets that city's Council change its hotel-tax rate by simple resolution, Mountain View's ordinance text (amending City Code Section 33.2(c)) requires the Council to act "by ordinance amending this section," a more formal legislative instrument than a resolution, though no source reviewed specifies additional procedural requirements, such as two readings or a waiting period, specific to this ordinance beyond a normal noticed council meeting. No additional voter approval, supermajority Council vote, or automatic index is required for the Council to raise the rate anywhere within the 10%-to-15% range once voters approve the ceiling. City staff have indicated they plan to bring a specific new rate to the Council for consideration in November or December 2026, but the measure does not require the Council to act on any timetable, or at all. The money itself is not controlled by any earmark, oversight board, or spending formula: because it is a general tax deposited into the General Fund, the City Council retains full discretion, through the annual budget process, over how the revenue is spent, notwithstanding the specific services listed in the ballot question. The City Council placed this measure on the ballot by a unanimous vote on June 23, 2026, following a staff recommendation from the City Manager's Office; the resolution and council report do not name an individual councilmember as the measure's sponsor.
loopholes: The ballot question and the argument in favor both cite the up-to-15% rate and the up-to-$5.2-million revenue figure prominently, but the measure's actual, immediate legal effect is nothing: the tax rate stays at 10% until the City Council separately adopts a future ordinance to raise it, on no fixed timetable and with no requirement that it ever do so.

The ballot question describes the revenue as funding specific services (potholes, police/fire/911 response, affordable housing, parks), but the City Attorney's Impartial Analysis confirms this is a general tax deposited into the General Fund and usable for "any general governmental purpose"; the named services are examples, not a binding earmark, and the City Council retains full discretion over how the revenue is actually spent through the normal annual budget process.

Because no primary argument against Measure F was filed with the Registrar of Voters, and no organized opposition campaign was identified in the sources reviewed, voters will encounter only the case in favor in the County Voter Information Guide, with no countervailing figures or arguments printed alongside it, unlike several other Santa Clara County measures on the same ballot.
unexpected_provisions: This measure does not itself raise the hotel tax at all; it only authorizes the City Council to raise it later, up to a 15% ceiling, at a public meeting after the election. A voter who reads only the $5.2 million ballot-question figure would not know that no new revenue is generated the day this measure passes, and that the actual increase depends on a separate Council decision not yet made.

The tax applies identically to short-term rental stays (Airbnb-style listings), not only traditional hotels and motels, using the same 10%-to-15% rate range and the same Council-authorization mechanism.

This TOT measure exists because the City Council originally planned to ask voters for a much larger $480-650 million general obligation bond, and only pivoted to a hotel-tax increase after three rounds of 2026 polling showed bond support falling well short of the two-thirds supermajority a bond requires; a voter would not learn this history from the ballot question itself.

This is legally a general tax whose proceeds voters cannot direct to the specific services named in the ballot question; a voter who supports the measure specifically to fund potholes, police, fire, or affordable housing has no legal guarantee the money will be spent that way rather than on any other lawful city purpose.

This is the second tax measure Mountain View has asked voters to approve in three election cycles; voters approved an increase to the city's property transfer tax in November 2024, which generated $5.1 million in the 2025-26 fiscal year, a context not mentioned in the Measure F ballot question.
pros: The tax is paid only by hotel, motel, and short-term rental guests staying fewer than 30 days; Mountain View residents pay no part of it directly, and supporters argue visitors who use city streets, parks, and public safety services during their stay should help fund them.

Mountain View's 10% hotel tax rate has not changed since 1991 and is among the lowest in Santa Clara County and the broader Bay Area; a city staff comparison found neighboring cities' rates ranging from about 12% (San Jose, Sunnyvale, Campbell) up to 15.5% (Palo Alto), and supporters argue the increase would simply bring Mountain View in line with comparable jurisdictions without harming hotel competitiveness.

Revenue stays with the City of Mountain View and, per the council report, is "generally protected from state reallocation," providing an ongoing General Fund source supporters say is needed for infrastructure, public safety, parks, and affordable housing priorities identified through a citywide community survey.

The measure lets the City Council calibrate the rate increase to actual conditions, rather than locking in a single number now, while voters retain control of the maximum rate (15%) that can ever be charged without a further vote.

At the full 15% rate, the increase could generate approximately $5.2 to $5.5 million a year according to the ballot question and the argument in favor, funding supporters say addresses top community priorities (streets and roads, public safety, affordable housing, parks) identified through a 1,257-response citywide survey, at no direct cost to residents.

Measure F requires annual independent audits of the revenue collected, and is supported by the full City Council as well as the League of Women Voters of the Los Altos-Mountain View Area, per the primary argument in favor.
cons: The City Council can raise the rate from the current 10% up to the full 15% ceiling on its own, by ordinance, without another public vote, meaning the tax burden hotel and short-term-rental guests ultimately pay is a decision made by city officials after the election rather than something voters directly approve at a specific number.

Because the money goes into the General Fund as a general tax, it is not legally restricted to the services listed in the ballot question, so voters have no enforceable guarantee the revenue will fund what the ballot title promises.

No primary argument against Measure F was filed with the Registrar of Voters, so the County Voter Information Guide will present only the case in favor, without a countervailing perspective on potential impacts to the local hotel industry or Mountain View's competitiveness as a lodging destination.

This is the second tax measure Mountain View voters have been asked to approve in the past three election cycles (after the November 2024 property transfer tax increase), which some residents and at least one Mountain View Voice commenter have characterized as an increasing tax burden, even though the burden of this particular measure falls on visitors rather than residents.

The measure was developed as a fallback after city-commissioned polling showed insufficient support for a much larger general obligation bond, using a different, non-hotel-tax-specific set of 2024 polling data rather than direct 2026 testing of the TOT proposal itself, according to public records obtained by the Mountain View Voice.

nonpartisan_analysis.source: City of Mountain View City Attorney, Impartial Analysis of Measure F
nonpartisan_analysis.summary: Confirms Measure F was placed on the ballot by a unanimous City Council vote and asks voters to authorize the Council to increase the Transient Occupancy Tax to a maximum of 15%, up from the current 10% (last changed in 1991). States the tax applies to hotels and short-term rentals alike, that revenue goes to the General Fund for any general governmental purpose (listing potholes, streets, police/fire/911 response, affordable housing, and parks only as examples), and that each 1-percentage-point increase could generate about $1.1 million a year. Confirms a 'no' vote keeps the rate at 10%, and a 'yes' vote only authorizes, but does not require, a future Council-adopted rate increase up to 15%.

Describes Measure F as a Mountain View City Council referral authorizing an increase of the city's hotel tax from 10% to a maximum of 15% to fund general city services, requiring a simple majority to pass, with full ordinance text available via the city's Legistar system.
